title: Four kinds of people (Avot 5:10)
hookLine: mine is mine and yours is yours; the saintly say mine is yours, the wicked say yours is mine

cards: Roommates. One labels every yogurt in the fridge with a name and a date. One eats everything, whoever bought it.

One quietly buys extra milk for the whole apartment and never mentions it. And one somehow always ends up with your charger, your hoodie and your leftovers, while his own stuff stays locked in his room.
Chapter five of Pirkei Avot sorts people into four kinds, by one simple question: what do you say about mine and yours?

teach.h: MINE IS MINE, YOURS IS YOURS.
teach.b: The one who says, what's mine is mine and what's yours is yours: that's the average person. Fair. Even.
Nobody owes anybody. The one who says, what's mine is yours and what's yours is mine: the simple, unlearned person. Friendly, but with no sense of boundaries.

The one who says, what's mine is yours, and what's yours is yours: the chasid, the saintly one, who gives freely and takes nothing. And the one who says, what's yours is mine and what's mine is mine: the wicked one.
Now the surprise, hidden in the first type.

teach.h: SOME SAY: THE WAY OF SODOM.
teach.b: The Mishnah adds: and some say, this is the way of Sodom. The perfectly fair one, like Sodom?
The rabbis remembered Sodom not only for its violence but as a city where nobody shared, where, the prophet Ezekiel says, the poor and needy were never helped.

teach.h: MINE IS YOURS: THE SAINTLY ONE.
teach.b: Mine is mine and yours is yours can be fair. Taken all the way, it's a world where no one ever gives anything. So the saying pushes past fairness.
What's mine is yours: that's the start of generosity, of giving without keeping score.
And that closes these weeks in Pirkei Avot, sayings from a chain of teachers reaching back to Sinai. Judge slowly. Three legs to stand on.
Open the door wide. Careful words. Pursue peace.
Care for yourself, care beyond yourself. Crouch down anyway. Everything else grows from the heart.
And today, what's mine is yours. Tomorrow opens the much bigger conversation this little tractate belongs to.

how: There is a custom of studying Pirkei Avot on Shabbat afternoons in the weeks after Passover, a chapter at a time, and its sayings are often discussed around the table.

o: the saintly one who gives freely and takes nothing
a person who keeps exactly to what's fair and even
a strict scholar who knows every law by heart

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.
p: mine is mine, yours is yours
mine is yours, yours is mine
mine is yours, yours is yours
yours is mine, mine is mine

s: the Mishnah praises mine is mine and yours is yours as the ideal
it calls it average, and some say it's the way of Sodom.
the saintly one gives freely and takes nothing
mine is yours, and yours is yours.
Ezekiel remembers Sodom as a city that didn't help the poor
the prophet says the poor and needy were never helped.

games.q: your roommate is short on groceries this week. you've always kept your shelves separate. what do you say?
o: mine is mine and yours is yours.
what's mine is yours. take what you need.
games.why: some in the Mishnah call strict mine-is-mine the way of Sodom. the saintly one says what's mine is yours.

practice: Think of a relationship where you quietly keep a ledger: who paid last time, who drove, who texted first, who did the dishes. Don't judge yourself; just notice the ledger.
Then imagine closing the book for one day, and giving time or help or a small thing you own with no note of it anywhere, not even in your head.

wordCard.voice: Chasid. The saintly one, who says what's mine is yours and what's yours is yours, giving freely and taking nothing. One of the four kinds of people, sorted by what they say about mine and yours.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: mine is yours and yours is yours, the way of the saintly one.

carryVoice: Your line: what's mine is yours. Fairness is the floor, not the goal. Two hundred sixty-eight days strong.
